rounds.take:
**First fork: one repo or several.** Every other Plan 1 question (layout, tooling, CI, naming, releases) sits inside this one, so it goes first.

Three settled facts in the handoff point the same way:

- **Adopters fork the repo, edit one config file and deploy with the included CI.** One fork has to contain the CDK app, the Lambdas it packages, the web bundle it uploads, the deployment skill and the workflows. With several repos, a fork means forking three or four repos and keeping their versions in step.
- **The web app reads a JSON Schema generated from the Python contract.** In one repo, CI regenerates the schema and fails the build if the committed copy drifts. Across repos, that becomes a published artifact plus a version bump on every contract change.
- **The backend imports the contract, and so does the local tool.** In one repo both use it from source. Several repos would make the contract a published package from day one, with release work before any real user exists.

There's a precedent on your machine: `bettor-help-platform` is one repo with a uv workspace for its Python packages (`packages/mcp-server`, `packages/portal-api`, ...) and npm for the CDK `infra` and the `portal` web app, all under one `ci.yml`.

What one repo gives up: the local tool can't have its own repo and issue tracker for researchers who never touch AWS. That doesn't block publishing: `pip install <tool>` still works from a monorepo, since each Python package builds its own wheel. A later split stays possible, because the contract and the tool are separate packages from the start.

The sketch below shows where each plan's work would sit. The folder names are placeholders: naming is a later card.

decisions.name: Kit name
decisions.question: What is the kit called: the repo, the docs title, and the prefix for its contract package and CDK construct?
decisions.example: An adopter reads the README and forks the repo; the contract installs as `<kit>-contract` and the construct is `<Kit>Archive`. `cruise` reads well, but it's taken on PyPI by an active project (a Linear agent tool, last release 2026-04-09), and it's a forestry term, which works against 'generic first'.

options.title: research-archive-in-a-box (descriptive)
options.includes: The repo keeps its current folder name. The docs say 'Research archive in a box'. The contract installs as `archive-contract`, the construct is `ResearchArchive`.
options.pulls_in: No collisions and says what it is, but it's long and not memorable. A short name can still be chosen later, at the cost of renaming.

options.title: quadrat
options.includes: A quadrat is the square frame a field researcher drops to sample one patch. Repo `quadrat`, contract `quadrat-contract`, construct `QuadratArchive`.
options.pulls_in: Short and free on PyPI and npm. An ecology word, so it leans toward the motivating field. GitHub user `quadrat` exists, but the repo lives under your own account.

options.title: cruise
options.includes: Your working idea: a timber cruise is a forest inventory survey. Repo `cruise`, contract `cruise-contract`.
options.pulls_in: Bare `cruise` is taken on PyPI and npm, so only prefixed names are free. Forestry-specific.

recommendation.why: It's the only option that's generic and collision-free today, and it's what the handoff and the folder already use. The kit is forked rather than installed, so its name matters less than the local tool's, which researchers type every day (DCSN2).

decisions.name: How cruise is installed
decisions.question: The tool is `cruise`. Do we publish it to PyPI, or do people install it straight from the repo?
decisions.example: A researcher wants `cruise audit ./my-dataset` on their laptop. Without PyPI, they run one uv command pointing at the GitHub repo. With PyPI they'd run `pip install <name>`, but bare `cruise` is taken there (another tool, active in 2026, which also installs a `cruise` command), so the PyPI name would have to differ from the command.

options.title: Not on PyPI: install from the repo with uv
options.includes: `uv tool install "git+https://github.com/<owner>/research-in-a-box#subdirectory=packages/tool"`, then `cruise audit .`. Inside the repo, `uv run cruise`. The package is named plain `cruise`, since it's never published. Releases are git tags and GitHub releases only.
options.pulls_in: No PyPI account, trusted publishing or name hunt. The docs say to use uv, since pip can't resolve the contract from the same repo. PyPI can still be added later if an outside user needs a plain `pip install`.

options.title: Publish to PyPI as cruise-cli
options.includes: `pip install cruise-cli`, then `cruise audit .`. The contract is published too, as `archive-contract`, since the tool depends on it.
options.pulls_in: A PyPI project for each of the two packages, trusted publishing in the release workflow, and a command name that differs from the install name.

options.title: Publish to PyPI as cruise-archive
options.includes: `pip install cruise-archive`, then `cruise audit .`, plus `archive-contract` as in B.
options.pulls_in: The same as B, and the name reads like the archive server rather than the local tool.

recommendation.why: No one outside this repo is installing cruise yet, and uv already installs it from git with the contract pulled from the same checkout (tested). That drops the PyPI release work and the name clash. Publishing stays a later, additive step.

decisions.question: Is a Python install enough for the local tool, or do we also ship a standalone app for people without Python?

With uv, `uv tool install accessioner` downloads a Python of its own and installs the tool, so the only prerequisite is the one-line uv installer. A standalone app would skip even that, but each OS needs its own build, and macOS and Windows need code signing so the app isn't blocked.

options.pulls_in: Nothing more to build. People who can't run any installer (a locked-down machine) aren't covered.

options.pulls_in: Three build jobs, an Apple Developer ID and a Windows signing certificate, and native dependencies (DuckDB, Pydantic's compiled core) bundled per platform.

options.pulls_in: Same as A today. The follow-up stays visible.

calls.name: GitHub Actions for CI
calls.question: Which CI does the kit ship with?
calls.took: GitHub Actions. The repo is on GitHub, adopters fork it there, and deploys reach AWS with GitHub OIDC (no stored keys).
calls.instead: A CI-neutral setup (scripts plus thin wrappers per CI), which means more files and a second path to test.
calls.why: The handoff assumes it, the family repos all use it, and nothing points to another CI.

evidence.output: CI is part of the kit. GitHub Actions is assumed and not yet confirmed.

calls.name: Folder layout
calls.question: Where does each part live in the repo?
calls.took: `packages/contract`, `packages/tool`, `packages/backend` (Python, uv workspace); `packages/infra` (CDK construct plus default app) and `packages/web` (React and Vite) (npm workspace); `agent/` (plugin, MCP server, skills); `examples/` (the sample package and an example archive config); `docs/`; `.github/workflows/`. Root holds `pyproject.toml`, `package.json`, `justfile`, `LICENSE`.
calls.instead: Top-level folders per part (`contract/`, `tool/`, `infra/`, `web/`) with no `packages/`, which is flatter but mixes code with docs and examples at the root.
calls.why: It matches the round you accepted and the bettor-help-platform precedent. Where the MCP server lives inside `agent/` is Plan 9's call.

calls.name: Python tooling
calls.question: Which Python tools?
calls.took: uv for packages, the lock and the workspace; ruff for lint and format; mypy in strict mode with the Pydantic plugin; pytest. Wheels built with hatchling. requires-python >=3.12 for every package; the backend runs on the newest Lambda Python runtime CDK offers.
calls.instead: pyright instead of mypy (faster, stricter inference), or a lower Python floor such as 3.11 for older lab machines.
calls.why: This is the set your Python repos already use (uv, ruff, mypy, pytest, hatchling), and mypy has a first-party Pydantic plugin.

calls.name: TypeScript tooling
calls.question: Which TypeScript tools?
calls.took: npm workspaces, TypeScript strict, ESLint (flat config), Prettier, Vitest for both the web app and the CDK construct tests.
calls.instead: pnpm, or Biome in place of ESLint and Prettier.
calls.why: npm is what bettor-help-platform uses alongside its CDK and portal, and Vitest serves both packages with one runner.

calls.name: One task runner
calls.question: How do people and CI run the checks?
calls.took: A root `justfile`: `just check` runs every lint, type check and test across Python and TypeScript, and CI runs exactly `just check`, path-filtered into Python and TypeScript jobs.
calls.instead: Separate commands per language, documented in the README.
calls.why: One command that CI and a person run identically means local and CI can't disagree.

calls.name: Schema drift check
calls.question: How does the web app's JSON Schema stay in step with the contract?
calls.took: The schema generated from the contract is committed under `packages/web/`, and `just check` regenerates it and fails when the committed copy differs.
calls.instead: Generate it at web build time only, with nothing committed. Simpler, but a contract change then shows up only as a web build or runtime error.
calls.why: Your rule: anything crossing Python to TypeScript is a generated contract that fails the build on drift.

calls.name: Versioning and releases
calls.question: How are versions numbered and released?
calls.took: One SemVer version for the whole repo, starting at 0.1.0. A `vX.Y.Z` tag makes a GitHub release with generated notes. Nothing is published to PyPI or npm; people install `cruise` from a tag with uv, and adopters deploy from their fork.
calls.instead: Per-package versions, so the tool can release without the archive. More flexible, more bookkeeping.
calls.why: Adopters fork the whole kit, so one version says which contract, tool and archive go together. DCSN2 dropped PyPI, and the handoff defers the npm library release.

calls.name: Contract as its own package
calls.question: Is the contract a package of its own?
calls.took: Yes: `archive-contract` (import `archive_contract`) is its own package in the uv workspace, and `cruise` and the backend depend on it through workspace sources. It isn't published anywhere.
calls.instead: Put the contract inside the tool's package. One fewer package, but the backend would then depend on the CLI.
calls.why: The backend, the tool and the MCP server all need the contract; only researchers need the CLI. A uv install from git resolves it from the same checkout (tested on DCSN2).

calls.name: Local folder keeps its name
calls.question: Does the local folder get renamed to research-in-a-box?
calls.took: No. The GitHub repo is `research-in-a-box`, and the local folder stays `research-archive-in-a-box` for now, because both planning folders (this one and Plan 2's) and their running sessions are recorded by that path.
calls.instead: Rename the folder now, then reopen both planning folders at the new path.
calls.why: Renaming under two live diazo folders breaks their recorded paths for no gain today. A rename can happen once the planning sessions are done.

approved.body:
# Repo layout and conventions for research-in-a-box

## Goal

Every other plan can assume one repo layout, one toolchain and one set of names, and an empty skeleton of that repo exists with its checks passing locally and in CI. No features are designed here.

## One repo

Everything lives in one repo, `research-in-a-box`: the Python contract, the local tool, the backend Lambdas, the CDK construct with its default app, the web app, the agent layer, the docs and the CI. An adopter forks this one repo, edits one config file and deploys. The web app's JSON Schema, the backend and the local tool all use the contract from source, with no published artifact between them.

Python packages form a uv workspace; TypeScript packages form an npm workspace. Both are declared at the repo root.

Rests on: AGNT2, DCSN1

## Folder layout

```
research-in-a-box/
  packages/
    contract/      Python: archive-contract, the Pydantic models (Plan 2)
    tool/          Python: cruise, the local tool (Plan 3)
    backend/       Python: the Lambda code (Plans 6 and 7)
    infra/         TypeScript: the CDK construct and the default app (Plan 4)
    web/           TypeScript: the React and Vite web app (Plan 8)
  agent/           the plugin, MCP server and skills (Plan 9)
  examples/        example archive config and, from Plan 2, the sample package
  docs/            specs, plans and user docs
  .github/workflows/
  pyproject.toml   uv workspace root
  package.json     npm workspace root
  justfile
  LICENSE          MIT
```

Each Python package keeps its code under `src/<import name>/` and its tests under `tests/`. Where the MCP server sits inside `agent/` is Plan 9's call.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  tool["packages/tool (cruise)"] --> contract["packages/contract (archive-contract)"]
  backend["packages/backend"] --> contract
  contract -- "generated JSON Schema" --> web["packages/web"]
  infra["packages/infra"] -- "packages" --> backend
  infra -- "uploads bundle" --> web
```

Rests on: AGNT2

## Names

| Thing | Name |
| --- | --- |
| The repo, and the docs title | `research-in-a-box` |
| The contract package and import | `archive-contract`, `archive_contract` |
| The CDK construct | `ResearchArchive` |
| The local tool: package, command and import | `cruise` |

`cruise` is never published, so the PyPI project of the same name doesn't matter. The only clash would be its `cruise` command if both were installed in one environment, and `uv tool install` gives each tool its own.

Rests on: DCSN1, DCSN2

## Installing cruise

`cruise` is installed from the repo with uv, at a release tag or the default branch:

```
uv tool install "git+https://github.com/<owner>/research-in-a-box@v0.1.0#subdirectory=packages/tool"
```

uv resolves `archive-contract` from the same checkout through the workspace source. Inside a clone, `uv run cruise` runs it. uv downloads a Python of its own, so a machine without Python needs only the uv installer. The docs name uv as the way to install; plain pip can't resolve the contract from the same repo. There is no standalone app.

Rests on: DCSN2, DCSN3, AGNT9

## Python tooling

- uv for dependencies, the lock file (`uv.lock`, committed) and the workspace.
- hatchling builds each package.
- ruff for lint and format.
- mypy in strict mode with the Pydantic plugin.
- pytest.
- `requires-python = ">=3.12"` for every package. The backend runs on the newest Lambda Python runtime that CDK offers, chosen in Plan 4.
- `archive-contract` is its own package; `cruise` and the backend depend on it through `[tool.uv.sources] archive-contract = { workspace = true }`.

Rests on: AGNT3, AGNT9

## TypeScript tooling

- npm workspaces, with `package-lock.json` committed.
- TypeScript in strict mode.
- ESLint with a flat config, and Prettier.
- Vitest for both the web app and the CDK construct tests.

Rests on: AGNT4

## One check command and CI

A root `justfile` holds the commands. `just check` runs every format check, lint, type check and test in both languages, plus the schema drift check. CI is GitHub Actions: on every push and pull request, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `just check`, split into a Python job and a TypeScript job that each run their half (`just check-python`, `just check-ts`). The job commands are the same recipes a person runs, so local and CI can't disagree.

Deploy workflows with GitHub OIDC to AWS are Plan 10a's.

Rests on: AGNT1, AGNT5

## Schema drift

The JSON Schema generated from the contract is committed under `packages/web/`. `just check` regenerates it and fails when the committed copy differs. In the skeleton the contract is empty, so the generator and the check exist with an empty schema, and Plan 2 fills them in.

Rests on: AGNT6

## Versioning and releases

One SemVer version covers the whole repo, starting at 0.1.0. A `vX.Y.Z` tag runs `.github/workflows/release.yml`, which makes a GitHub release with generated notes. Nothing is published to PyPI or npm. People install `cruise` from a tag, and adopters deploy from their fork.

Rests on: AGNT7, DCSN2

## Risk and cost

Risk: low. The work creates a new, empty repo; a mistake is undone by editing or deleting files, and nothing outside the repo changes. Creating the GitHub repo is the one outward step, and it is a single step for you.

Cost: one step for you (creating the GitHub repo and pushing). The new programs are the ones named above (uv, just, Node and npm), which this machine already uses in other repos.

Rests on: AGNT1, DCSN1

## Left out

- Any feature design, and any code beyond empty packages and the checks.
- The sample package: Plan 2 builds it once the format exists. No data is committed by this plan.
- Publishing to PyPI or npm, and any standalone app.
- Deploy workflows, OIDC and the deployment skill (Plan 10a).
- Where the MCP server runs (Plan 9) and which Lambda runtime version (Plan 4).

Rests on: DCSN2, DCSN3

## How we'll know it works

- A fresh clone runs `just check` and it exits 0.
- The CI workflow on GitHub runs the same checks on the first push, and both jobs pass.
- `uv tool install` from the pushed repo installs a `cruise` command that runs (it prints its version).
- Each check fails when it should: a lint error, a type error, a failing test and a stale schema each make `just check` exit non-zero.
- Plan 2's folder has been told the layout and the contract's package name.

Rests on: AGNT5, AGNT6, DCSN2

approved.body:
# PLAN1: An empty, passing skeleton of research-in-a-box

## Spec

`docs/specs/2026-11-12-repo-layout-and-conventions/spec.md`, approved 2026-11-12.

## The change

Turn the project folder into a git repo holding the approved layout: a uv workspace with three empty Python packages (`archive-contract`, `cruise`, backend), an npm workspace with an empty CDK construct and an empty Vite web app, a schema generator with its drift check, one `just check` that runs every check, and the CI and release workflows. Then push it to a new public GitHub repo, `schuettc/research-in-a-box`, and confirm CI passes and `cruise` installs from it.

Each package holds only enough code for its checks to be able to fail: `cruise --version` prints the version, the contract's schema generator writes an empty schema, and the construct synthesises an empty stack.

Risk: low. Everything is new files in a new repo. A mistake is undone by editing or deleting files; the one outward step, creating the public GitHub repo, waits on your Go (STEP1).

## Left out

- Any feature code: the contract models, the tool's commands, Lambdas, resources in the construct and screens in the web app.
- The sample package (Plan 2), deploy workflows and OIDC (Plan 10a).
- Publishing to PyPI or npm.
- Renaming the local folder (call AGNT10).
- Committing other plans' planning folders: each planning session commits its own.

## Where
